Schedule POC kickoff with Parallax infra team for deployment window week of 11/24

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: 62m | Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Samir (SE), Lina, Rory; Ben (CTO), Maya (ML), Diego (SRE), Priya (Product), External Reviewer (Legal)

[00:00] Ava: ok, hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — deep dive on where to put the content safety checks, perf implications, kv cache and batching impact, and then ops questions for VPC/on-prem. we'll try to run 45 minutes of tech and 15 for ops/legal.
[00:22] Ben: sounds good. we're mainly worried about tail latency spikes when moderation fires, and cost creep. our users are clinicians so mistakes are bad.
[00:35] Samir: absolutely. by moderation you mean the safety classifier + heuristics we talked about, run either inline in the generation path or as a proxy side-service, right?
[00:46] Maya: yes. current infra: internal API -> Redwood hosted dedicated endpoint. we were going to pipeline moderation as a separate microservice currently, but open to options.
[00:55] Rory: for us, predictability is king. we can't have 99.9 degrade below SLA when a single flagged request triggers a heavy eval.
[01:12] Lina: quick note: provenance and audit logs matter too — we need per-token logs for flagged content for compliance. that will affect storage/ingest.
[01:30] Samir: ok, i'll start with numbers. inline placement means safety check runs inside the same request execution thread: advantage is fewer network hops and lower total p99 for short sequences. downside is that heavy checks block the GPU warm path, increasing latency variance and potentially reducing throughput because it prevents batching optimizing.
[01:52] Ben: can you quantify? ballpark cost/latency penalty?
[01:58] Samir: rough numbers from previous infra: for a 4k context generation at 16 tokens/sec effective, an inline light safety filter (binary classifier) adds ~6-12 ms median, ~15-40 ms p99 depending on model. heavier multimodal or multi-pass heuristics push median to 30-80 ms and p99 to 250-400 ms in worst case. when inline, that 400 ms sits on the critical path so requests can't be batched as efficiently.
[02:30] [02:30] Ben: that's bigger than we thought.
[02:33] Priya: what's proxy/protection placement then?
[02:36] Samir: proxy (we'll call it external filter) means request leaves the inference path, hits a separate service. pros: you can autoscale and isolate CPU-bound or specialized checkers, offload expensive heuristics to separate infra (maybe CPU elastic pools). cons: extra network hop, additional serialization, and potential consistency issues with KV cache state — especially if the safety step needs final token state.
[03:05] Diego: can the proxy see the same KV cache state? if safety needs to rerun with final prefix, it might need access to the model's KV cache, which lives on the TPU/GPU node. networks make that messy.
[03:20] Samir: yes, that's a big point. with Redwood's KV cache you can snapshot or share prefixes, but cross-service KV access costs: either copy the prefix over the network (adds latency) or co-locate the proxy on same node using in-memory IPC (operationally heavier). So we often recommend two modes: async proxy for first-pass filtering (fast, coarse) and inline last-pass for high-risk items.
[03:48] Maya: can you explain async vs sync proxy?
[03:51] Samir: async = you stream generation back to user quickly, mark as pending, and then run a background, heavier filter that may redact or flag content post-hoc. sync proxy = you block before returning final output until filter completes. async reduces perceived latency but complicates UX and compliance.
[04:10] Ben: hmm, compliance wants final check before show. healthcare regs tend to want pre-delivery checks for PHI leakage.
[04:18] External Reviewer (Legal): yes, for certain classes we prefer blocking. but we can allow async for low-risk transcripts if logged and reversible.
[04:30] Samir: important tradeoff. let me show a simple measured example from a previous benchmark (note: numbers fuzzy, for illustration): baseline generation p50=120ms p95=240ms p99=420ms. Add inline lightweight filter: p50=130ms p95=260ms p99=460ms. Add inline heavy multi-pass: p50=160ms p95=400ms p99=950ms. If you move heavy check to proxy sync with network hop + 30ms: p50=150ms p95=280ms p99=600ms but proxy can autoscale so p95 rarely spikes as much.
[05:10] Priya: ok, so sometimes proxy wins on p99 because it isolates the GPU path?
[05:16] Samir: Exactly. But micro-architectural details matter: batching, tokenization, and KV cache usage. If proxy requires access to internal KV state to run an accurate check, copying that state can be tens to hundreds of ms for long contexts.
[05:34] Ben: what about caching results of safety checks? like if identical prompts seen often.
[05:40] Lina: we do prompt fingerprinting today for some heuristics. Samir?
[05:42] Samir: yes, prefix caching helps. Redwood supports prefix-level KV caching and a safety cache index. If you can deterministically map a prefix to a safety decision, you can short-circuit expensive checks. In practice, cache hit rates vary — for customer data with many unique clinical notes, hit rates may be low (5-12%). But for templated UI flows, hit rates can be >50%.
[06:06] Diego: how much does caching reduce overhead?
[06:09] Samir: overall end-to-end latency reduces by the cost of the safety pass. So if a heavy safety pass costs +200ms, a cache hit saves that 200ms. On throughput, caching lets the GPU do more batching by reducing blocking calls.
[06:25] Ben: batching — we use Redwood batching config. how does batching interact with safety checks?
[06:30] Samir: continuous batching aggregates tokens across requests. Inline blocking checks break the batching window and may flush the batch early, reducing throughput efficiency and raising cost per token. Proxy checks do not block GPU batching unless they require synchronous KV reads/writes. Quantization also matters: int8/4-bit quantization reduces model latency and memory footprint, which indirectly reduces the marginal cost of inline checks because generation path is faster, but the relative overhead of safety checks (often CPU-bound) can become a larger percentage.
[07:05] Maya: can Redwood recommend a config tuned for healthcare?
[07:09] Samir: yes — we typically recommend a hybrid: lightweight inline filter (fast classifier) + sync proxy for higher-risk classes. Use aggressive prefix caching and token-level audit logs enabled asynchronously. For infra: Dedicated pools with reserved capacity to avoid noisy neighbor spikes and conservative autoscale thresholds so that when heavy checks occur we have headroom.
[07:34] Priya: headroom costs money — can we simulate cost vs latency tradeoffs?
[07:38] Samir: yes, that's what Redwood Optimize does. we run model-by-workload simulations — we can show cost per 1M tokens for different configs (inline-only, proxy-only, hybrid) and different batch sizes.
[07:50] Ben: please do. also we need quantization guidance — are there safety regressions with 4-bit quant?
[07:56] Samir: good question. quantization can affect classifier accuracy if the safety model is also quantized or if the main model's output distribution shifts. Redwood's approach: keep safety classifier on a separate, higher-precision instance (FP16) when safety fidelity is critical, or retrain/calibrate thresholds for quantized generation. We can provide regression test harnesses.
[08:20] Diego: on VPC/on-prem, will Redwood Private let us keep the safety proxy inside our network to avoid egress?
[08:27] Ava: yes, Redwood Private supports deploying the control plane in your VPC and we can co-locate proxy components inside customer network. Many customers deploy the safety proxy as a customer-managed service with Redwood routing policies.
[08:40] Diego: any certs or KMS integrations required?
[08:44] Ava: KMS, HSM are supported; we also do SIEM/ELK log forwarding and audit log exports. we'll share the security pack.
[08:54] Maya: what about fallback and graceful degradation? If safety infra is overloaded, do you have default policies?
[08:59] Samir: yes. Redwood supports policy-based fallback: fallback-mode can be (a) degrade to simpler model variant, (b) apply strict conservative redact, or (c) return an error. We recommend conservative redact with a clear UX cue in healthcare; also enable alerts so SREs can scale proactively.
[09:20] Ben: curious about numbers: in a mixed workload we saw a 35% throughput drop when heavy inline checks were enabled in our tests. is that consistent?
[09:29] Samir: that aligns with other customers — throughput delta depends on check profile and batch sizes. For small interactive queries (few tokens), overhead is relatively higher. For long-streaming outputs, overhead amortizes over tokens.
[09:46] Priya: streaming — do safety checks run per token or after full output?
[09:50] Samir: both patterns exist. Token-level inline checks are expensive. Common pattern: run coarse token-level heuristics inline (fast), then post-hoc full-output checks in proxy. For streaming UX, you can stream initial content with a promise to redact or modify if later checks fail. Must weigh compliance.
[10:10] [10:10] Ben: any notes on observability? we need token-level latency breakdown and per-route cost.
[10:15] Lina: Console provides per-route breakdown and tracing hooks. We can add custom tracing tags at the filter boundary to measure exactly how much time was spent in safety logic vs model generation vs network.
[10:29] Samir: also we instrument cache hit/miss rates and provide histograms for p50/p95/p99. We'll attach example dashboards.
[10:38] Diego: about KV cache replication — can we keep a warm shard copy for the proxy to avoid copying full prefix?
[10:45] Samir: there are two approaches: prefix snapshot replication (copy the minimal prefix required for the check) or shared in-memory store co-located with the GPU (fast IPC). Snapshot replication favors easier ops but adds latency; shared memory has low latency but is operationally complex and may not be feasible in Private on-prem setups without infra changes.
[11:08] Priya: what's the recommended approach for our expected 20k qps peak?
[11:12] Samir: for 20k qps with mostly short responses, dedicated capacity with multiple pod replicas, aggressive batching, and hybrid safety (light inline + sync proxy for flagged classes) is best. Also use routing policies that send high-risk routes to reserved pools so they don't affect general traffic.
[11:34] Ben: what about cost math — estimate monthly cost difference between inline heavy checks and hybrid?
[11:39] Samir: we promised a spreadsheet; preliminary: heavy inline might increase GPU-hours by 25-40% due to decreased batching efficiency; hybrid shifts some compute to CPU/elastic pools and can reduce GPU-hours by ~10-20% but adds CPU billing. net cost often comparable or slightly lower with hybrid for heavy safety workloads. we'll send explicit numbers.
[11:59] Maya: curious if Redwood has any recommendations for filter implementation to be faster?
[12:03] Samir: yes: 1) move expensive heuristics off the critical GPU path; 2) use smaller dedicated safety models (fast classifiers) trained to high recall; 3) use approximate methods (hashing/fingerprints) as pre-filters; 4) maintain a safety cache; 5) calibrate thresholds per customer.
[12:23] Diego: is there support for running our proprietary classifier inside Redwood Private as a sidecar?
[12:28] Ava: yes, Redwood Private allows customer-managed sidecars and we have patterns to integrate them into routing. you retain control and keys.
[12:35] Priya: legal: if we run customer code in sidecar, how is audit handled?
[12:40] External Reviewer (Legal): auditor access and logs must be retained; we need clear contract clauses about responsibility and data ownership.
[12:49] Ava: we'll include standard contract language and we can add specific clauses.
[12:55] [12:55] Ben: any risk of safety classifier model drift if we quantize or update base generator?
[13:01] Samir: yes — changes in generation distribution can change safety metric operating point. Redwood recommends regression testing on a stable prompt corpus before each model roll and use eval alerts to detect drift.
[13:17] Priya: can Redwood run those evals as a managed service?
[13:20] Samir: yes, Redwood Optimize provides regular evals tied to prompts and can alert on quality regressions.
[13:30] Ben: latency SLO targets — what's realistic with hybrid approach?
[13:34] Samir: realistic p95 under hybrid for short responses is ~200-350ms depending on model size and batch config. p99 is tougher but we can target 500-650ms with reserved capacity and conservative autoscale.
[13:50] Diego: what about burst capacity — do you have cold-start issues when safety proxy scales up?
[13:55] Samir: to avoid cold-start latency we recommend pre-warmed pools and fast-start containers. Redwood Dedicated supports burst capacity options to cover spikes with lower latency.
[14:10] Priya: are there any quick wins we can apply immediately?
[14:13] Samir: yes — enable fast classifier inline, enable safety cache for templated prompts, and set conservative autoscale thresholds on Dedicated. We can help tune these in the POC.
[14:25] Ben: good. can we walk through an example trace end-to-end?
[14:29] Samir: sure — imagine a clinician query: User -> Parallax API -> Redwood route -> generation starts, preliminary inline classifier runs after prompt + 50 tokens (fast binary) -> no flag so we continue streaming. Meanwhile background proxy runs a full-output check using copied prefix snapshot; if flagged, it issues a redact patch via callback. In blocking mode, the proxy would block the final commit until check passes.
[15:05] Maya: how do you patch/redact?
[15:07] Samir: there's an API for post-hoc edits: redact token spans and send an updated version to the client with an audit event. UX work needed.
[15:19] Priya: that patching seems tricky for real-time clinical flows.
[15:23] Samir: agreed — that's why for PHI-sensitive flows we recommend sync proxy for final check.
[15:30] Ben: any data on classifier false positives impacting UX?
[15:34] Samir: FP rates vary — aggressive classifiers minimize FNs at cost of FPs. You should tune threshold and use human-in-the-loop for borderline cases, at least at rollout.
[15:48] [15:48] Diego: about telemetry — do you offer token-level redaction diff logs?
[15:52] Lina: yes, can export redaction diffs and event audit streams to customer SIEM.
[15:59] Ben: what's a reasonable POC scope?
[16:02] Ava: run bench with your sample corpus, deploy hybrid safety on a staging route in your VPC, validate compliance logs and UI redact flow, and test failover policies. We'll aim for a 2-3 week POC.
[16:16] Ben: timeline looks ok. we'll need procurement to sign NDA.
[16:20] Ava: we'll send the NDA and contract checklist.
[16:23] [16:23] Priya: any gotchas for on-prem?
[16:26] Samir: on-prem requires careful kernel selection for inference, quantization toolchain compatibility, and resource planning for KV cache. Also you lose some hosted observability unless you connect telemetry exports.
[16:40] Ben: can you share a sample dashboard and the benchmark sheet?
[16:44] Samir: yes — pushing link to the deck and sheet in the calendar invite now: https://redwood.example.com/decks/moderation-overhead and spreadsheet: https://redwood.example.com/bench/moderation-oht.
[16:58] [16:58] Maya: will the bench include both sync and async proxy scenarios?
[17:01] Samir: yes — we'll run inline-light, inline-heavy, proxy-sync, proxy-async, hybrid, with/without KV snapshots, and quantization variants.
[17:12] Diego: please include network cost estimates for KV snapshots.
[17:15] Samir: will do.
[17:18] Ben: ok, any more technical details on KV snapshot sizes?
[17:22] Samir: snapshot size roughly scales with sequence length and hidden size; e.g., for a 4k context on a 16k model hidden state, snapshot could be tens of MBs; for typical 2k context it's single-digit MBs. Transferring 10MB adds ~10-50ms depending on network.
[17:44] Priya: are there options to compress the snapshot?
[17:47] Samir: yes — sparse snapshots or compressed float16 transfers reduce size. There's tradeoff with CPU cost to compress/decompress. We'll test compression in the bench.
[17:58] [17:58] Ben: earlier you said inline heavy increases p99 to near 1s. that's concerning. Is that with any mitigation?
[18:03] Samir: mitigations: prioritize safety threads lower so they don't block generation path? That risks returning unsafe content. Better: run approximate check inline and run full check in proxy, or reserve headroom and add rapid scale-up.
[18:20] Diego: what about throttling flagged flows to slow them down?
[18:22] Samir: yes you can throttle or route flagged flows to dedicated pools to avoid impacting general traffic.
[18:30] Priya: let's discuss fallback modes and UX language for clinicians.
[18:34] External Reviewer (Legal): we prefer explicit messaging: "Content withheld pending review" and retention of original content in audit logs.
[18:42] Ben: ok. how do we sign off on the POC success criteria?
[18:45] Ava: propose success criteria: 1) p95 latency within 300ms for standard flows, 2) p99 less than 650ms for hybrid on staging, 3) no data egress violations, 4) audit logs available and parsable.
[19:02] Maya: agreed.
[19:05] Samir: technical note: we'll add a tracing header to correlate request->safety-check->cache-hit paths to compute exact overhead per request.
[19:14] Ben: that will help.
[19:18] [19:18] Priya: any implementation risk with our internal prompt templates?
[19:21] Samir: templated prompts often increase cache hits — good for you. but if they are dynamically filled with free text, less so. we can advise minor prompt refactoring to increase determinism where possible.
[19:36] Diego: ops question — firewall rules and VPC peering. Ava?
[19:40] Ava: we'll provide network diagram and required egress ports; for Private we'll do peering/Direct Connect options.
[19:48] Ben: do you have examples of other healthcare customers?
[19:51] Ava: yes, we reference anonymized case studies — we'll share them with NDA.
[19:56] [19:56] Priya: ok last bit: monitoring alerts thresholds and runbooks?
[20:00] Lina: we'll provide sample alerts for safety-fail-rate, cache-miss spike, p99 latency. also a runbook for fallback modes.
[20:10] Ben: great. I want to flag data residency — some content must never leave EU. how does proxy handle region routing?
[20:17] Samir: Redwood routing policies support region pinning and can route EU data to EU-only pools or to Private. We'll include region config examples.
[20:30] Maya: can we get an estimate for infra changes for co-locating proxy with GPU nodes?
[20:34] Samir: co-locating requires changes to pod spec and memory footprint; ops overhead higher but latency lower. We'll quantify in bench.
[20:45] [20:45] Ben: ok, summary?
[20:47] Ava: recap: Redwood will run bench matrix, send security pack and dashboard, propose POC plan for week of 11/24. customer to share corpus and peering windows. we agreed hybrid approach as initial config.
[21:05] Ben: any other questions?
[21:07] Priya: none from product.
[21:09] External Reviewer (Legal): please include redaction policy template.
[21:12] Ava: will do.
[21:14] Samir: i'll follow up with bench results and include compression and kv snapshot numbers.
[21:18] Ben: thanks everyone.
[21:20] Ava: thanks, we'll follow up. closing.

--- END TRANSCRIPT ---

References shared during call: deck link (see calendar), benchmark sheet: https://redwood.example.com/bench/moderation-oht, security pack link: https://redwood.example.com/security/parallax-pack.pdf

Call recap (auto): Hybrid safety (inline fast classifier + sync proxy for high-risk) recommended; KV cache snapshot tradeoffs and compression explored; POC and benchmarks agreed; deliverables: bench spreadsheet, security docs, POC plan.

Explicit next steps (from transcript):
- Redwood to run the bench runs across inline-heavy, inline-light, proxy-sync, proxy-async, hybrid, with and without KV snapshots and quantization variants.
- Parallax to provide sample prompt corpus and peak qps.
- Schedule POC week of 2025-11-24.

End of file
